ex-absolute-versus-relative-singular-val.actual_claim_text: Let $B=\operatorname{diag}(1,\epsilon)$ with $0<\epsilon<1$. A perturbation of spectral norm $\epsilon$ can change the small singular value to zero, giving relative error one. A componentwise relative perturbation of size $\eta$ instead changes it by relative error exactly $\eta$, independently of how small $\epsilon$ is. Thus the absolute guarantee and the stronger bidiagonal relative guarantee answer different questions.

current_proof_steps.text: The singular values of $B$ are $1$ and $\epsilon$. Set $E_0=\operatorname{diag}(0,-\epsilon)$. Then $B+E_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, $\|E_0\|_2=\epsilon$, and the small singular value changes by absolute error $\epsilon$ and relative error $\epsilon/\epsilon=1$. This attains the absolute bound in [F1]. [F1, algebra]

Set $E_1=\eta B$. Each nonzero diagonal entry is multiplied by $1+\eta$ and the zero superdiagonal remains zero, so [F2] applies. Directly, $B+E_1=(1+\eta)B$, whose small singular value is $(1+\eta)\epsilon$ and whose relative error is exactly $\eta$. [F2, algebra]

Since $\eta$ can be fixed while $\epsilon$ tends to zero, step 1.2 gives a relative guarantee independent of the small singular value; step 1.1 shows that the absolute error scale alone permits complete loss of that value. [step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

ex-nearly-rank-deficient-design-matrix.actual_claim_text:
For $\epsilon=10^{-8}$, let the design matrix be
$$A_\epsilon=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&\epsilon\end{pmatrix}.$$
Its exact rank is two, but its spectral numerical rank is one at tolerance $10^{-7}$ and two at tolerance $10^{-9}$.

current_proof_steps.text: The determinant of $A_\epsilon$ is $\epsilon\ne0$, so its exact rank is two. By [F2], write $A_\epsilon=U\Sigma V^*$; taking determinants and using $|\det U|=|\det V|=1$ (from $U^*U=V^*V=I$) gives $\sigma_1\sigma_2=\epsilon$. Its first column has norm one, hence [F4] gives $\sigma_1=\|A_\epsilon\|_2\ge1$; by [F3], $\sigma_1\le\|A_\epsilon\|_F=\sqrt{2+\epsilon^2}<2$. Therefore $\epsilon/2<\sigma_2\le\epsilon$. [F2, F3, F4, algebra]

At $\tau=10^{-7}$, $\sigma_2\le10^{-8}<\tau<1\le\sigma_1$, so exactly one singular value exceeds $\tau$. At $\tau=10^{-9}$, $\sigma_2>5\cdot10^{-9}>\tau$ and $\sigma_1\ge1>\tau$, so both exceed $\tau$. [step 1.1, algebra]
Applying [F1] to the two counts in step 2.1 gives numerical ranks one and two, respectively, although the exact rank remains two. [step 2.1, F1] ∎

lem-exact-householder-bidiagonal-reducti.actual_claim_text: For $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, the exact-arithmetic algorithm [[alg-householder-bidiagonalization]] returns unitary $U,V$ and an upper bidiagonal $B\in\mathbb F^{p\times p}$, $p=\min(m,n)$, such that if $m\ge n$ then $U^*AV=\begin{bmatrix}B\\0\end{bmatrix}$, and if $m<n$ then $U^*A^*V=\begin{bmatrix}B\\0\end{bmatrix}$.

current_proof_steps.text: At step $k$, the left reflector acts only on rows $k:M$. It therefore leaves all rows $1,\ldots,k-1$ unchanged and maps the active part of column $k$ to its first coordinate, making entries below $(k,k)$ zero. The right reflector acts only on columns $k+1:p$, so it preserves the zeros already made in column $k$ and maps the active part of row $k$ to its first coordinate, making entries beyond $(k,k+1)$ zero. [F1, F2]

Subsequent left reflectors act on rows strictly below row $k$, so they do not change row $k$; subsequent right reflectors act on columns strictly beyond column $k+1$, so they do not change its retained first two entries. Induction on $k$ shows the final transformed matrix has no entries below the diagonal or beyond the first superdiagonal in its first $p$ rows. [step 1.1, F1, induction]

The update rules in [F1] maintain the invariant $C=U^*C_0V$, where $C_0$ is the initial tall-oriented matrix. Every factor is unitary by [F2], so the accumulated $U,V$ are unitary. Combining this invariant with step 2.1 gives the asserted tall reduction. In the wide case it applies to $A^*$, and taking adjoints gives $A=V\begin{bmatrix}B^*&0\end{bmatrix}U^*$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

lem-implicit-bidiagonal-qr-bulge-chase-u.actual_claim_text: Consider one exact-arithmetic sweep of [[alg-implicit-shifted-bidiagonal-qr-with-deflation]] on an unreduced upper bidiagonal block, with no nonzero deflation. If its right rotations have product $V_s$ and its left rotations have product $U_s$, the restored bidiagonal block is $B_+=U_s^*BV_s$. Consequently $B_+$ and $B$ have the same singular values. If a set $D$ of superdiagonal entries is deflated, then the transformed output instead equals the corresponding unitary transform of $B+E_D$, where $E_D$ has those entries negated and all other entries zero.

current_proof_steps.text: The first right rotation acts on the leading adjacent column pair of the active block and creates at most the first subdiagonal bulge. Each left rotation annihilates the current subdiagonal entry; because it mixes only two adjacent rows, it can create at most the next second-superdiagonal bulge. The following right rotation mixes only the adjacent columns supporting that bulge, annihilates it, and creates at most the next subdiagonal bulge. Induction along the block therefore keeps one bulge at a time and removes it at the next alternating rotation. The zero coupling at a deflated block endpoint prevents a bulge from leaving the block, so the final matrix is upper bidiagonal. [F1, F2, induction]

Every right operation multiplies on the right by a unitary Givens factor and every left operation multiplies on the left by the adjoint of a unitary Givens factor. Their products therefore give unitary $U_s,V_s$ and the final matrix is exactly $U_s^*BV_s$. [F1, F2, algebra]

Left and right unitary factors preserve singular values, since $(U_s^*(B+E_D)V_s)^*(U_s^*(B+E_D)V_s)=V_s^*(B+E_D)^*(B+E_D)V_s$ is unitarily similar to $(B+E_D)^*(B+E_D)$. Deflation occurs before the sweep rotations, and setting each listed superdiagonal entry to zero adds exactly its negative there; hence the matrix entering the unitary sweep is $B+E_D$. With no deflation $E_D=0$, so step 1.2 gives equal singular values for $B_+$ and $B$. [step 1.2, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

lem-scaled-complex-householder-and-given.actual_claim_text:
Use [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]] successfully, with $0<u<1$ and $(r-1)u<1$ for every Householder dimension $r$. For a nonzero Householder column define
$$e=(1+u)^{r+3}-1,\quad a_\phi=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^4}-1,\quad a_\alpha=(1+a_\phi)(1+e)(1+u)-1,\quad d_v=a_\alpha+u(2+a_\alpha),$$
$$a_\tau=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^{2r}}-1,\quad g=\frac{1+6u}{1-(r-1)u}-1,\quad c_U=2\bigl((1+a_\tau)(1+u)(1+6u)(1+g)-1\bigr),$$
$$\eta_H(r)=\max\{a_\alpha+8d_v,(1+u)c_U+3u\}.$$
For a Givens step define
$$a_2=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^2}-1,\quad q=\max\left\{\left(\frac{1+u}{1-u}\right)^3-1,\frac{(1+a_2)(1+6u)(1+u)}{(1-u)^3}-1\right\},$$
$$\epsilon=\sqrt2(7u+6u^2)(1+q),\quad v=q+\epsilon,\quad \eta_G=2v+u+2q.$$
Each complete left update, including its target zero write, has an exact unitary representative $W$ and perturbation $E$ with
$$W(C+E)=C_+,\qquad \|E\|_F\le\eta\|C\|_F,$$
where $\eta=\eta_H(r)$ or $\eta_G$. Identity branches have $E=0$. The corresponding right relation follows by conjugate transposition. For a Givens application without an annihilation overwrite use the smaller coefficient $v$; for a Householder separate-block application use $(1+u)c_U+3u$. All coefficients are explicit and $O(ru)$ or $O(u)$ for fixed dimensions.

current_proof_steps.text: A complex product's real/imaginary error is at most $2(2u+u^2)|z||w|\le6u|z||w|$: bound each of its four real products and then its two component additions. A sequential complex dot of length $r$ therefore has error at most $[6u+\gamma_{r-1}(1+6u)]\sum_i|z_i||w_i|=g\sum_i|z_i||w_i|$. These expansions include exact zeros. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

A scaled norm with $2r$ real components has its positive squared sum multiplied termwise by between $(1-u)^{2r+2}$ and $(1+u)^{2r+2}$, including two scaling factors. Square root and rescaling give relative norm error at most $e$. The independently scaled modulus of $x_1$ has lower/upper factors $(1-u)^4,(1+u)^4$, so the phase division error relative to $x_1/|x_1|$ is at most $a_\phi$; when $x_1=0$ it is zero. Thus for $N=\|x\|$, $\alpha_0=-\operatorname{phase}(x_1)N$ and $v_0=x-\alpha_0e_1$, one has $|\widehat\alpha-\alpha_0|\le a_\alpha N$ and $\|v-v_0\|\le d_vN$. For exponents at least one the lower deviation is bounded by the upper by convexity, justifying these two-sided estimates. [F1, F2, algebra]

The identity $H(v)^*H(v)=I$ follows by multiplying $I-2vv^*/(v^*v)$. The exact phase choice gives $H(v_0)x=\alpha_0e_1$ and $\|v_0\|\ge N$ by direct inner-product expansion. Normalization gives $\|a/\|a\|-b/\|b\|\|\le2\|a-b\|/\|b\|$; expanding the difference of unit-vector projectors therefore gives $\|H(v)-H(v_0)\|\le8d_v$. The target-column error is at most $(a_\alpha+8d_v)N$. [step 1.2, algebra]

For Givens formation at stored $z,w$, the norm $h$ has relative factors between $(1-u)^3$ and $(1+u)^3$, since its unscaled four-component squared sum has at most four rounding factors per term. The norm $n_z$ has exponents two. Let $G_0$ be the exact canonical Givens annihilator for $(z,w)$, with coefficients $c_0=|z|/\|(z,w)\|$ and $s_0=(z/|z|)\overline w/\|(z,w)\|$ when $z\ne0$. The phase error is at most $a_2$; the coefficient numerator, denominator, six-operation complex product and division errors therefore give $|c-c_0|\le q c_0$ and $|s-s_0|\le q|s_0|$. If $z=0$, $c=0$ and $s_0=\overline w/|w|$; the smaller bound $(1+u)/(1-u)^3-1\le q$ applies. Hence $\|(c,s)-(c_0,s_0)\|\le q$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

The positive real sum defining $w$ has bounds $(1-u)^{2r}\|v\|^2\le w\le(1+u)^{2r}\|v\|^2$. The final division gives $|\widehat\tau\|v\|^2/2-1|\le a_\tau$. The dot-product error in step 1.1, the componentwise real multiplication by $\widehat\tau$ and the final complex multiplication bound the rank-one update error by $c_U\|B\|_F$. Final subtraction adds at most $u(3+c_U)\|B\|_F$. Combine this with step 2.1 over disjoint columns to get the Householder bound. For the zero column take the identity exactly. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

Put $t=\sqrt{c^2+|s|^2}>0$ and $Q=T/t$. Direct multiplication gives $T^*T=t^2I$, so $Q$ is canonical unitary, $\|T-Q\|=|t-1|\le q$ and $\|T\|\le1+q$. Normalization also gives $\|Q-G_0\|\le2q$; differences of canonical blocks have norm equal to the Euclidean norm of their coefficient differences. Each computed output entry has error at most $(7u+6u^2)(|c||C_{1j}|+|s||C_{2j}|)$, by two products and their addition. The absolute coefficient block has norm at most $\sqrt2t$. Thus the raw update differs from $QC$ by at most $v\|C\|_F$. [step 2.2, algebra]

Scaling introduced $\|\lambda(z,w)-(a,b)\|\le u\|(a,b)\|$. Because $G_0$ annihilates $(z,w)$, its exact target residual for $(a,b)$ is at most $u\|(a,b)\|$; under $Q$ it is at most $(u+2q)\|(a,b)\|$. Writing the rounded target to zero adds at most $(u+2q+v)\|(a,b)\|$ to the raw update discrepancy, so the total is at most $\eta_G\|C\|_F$. No unrelated matrix entry is zeroed for a shift-vector rotation. Identity branches have zero discrepancy. [F1, step 2.2, step 3.2, algebra]

In every left case choose $E=W^*C_+-C$, with $W=H(v)$ or $Q$; unitarity gives the stated equation and equal error norm. Right updates follow by conjugate transposition and invariance of Frobenius norm. All coefficients are finite explicit functions under the stated conditions, vanish at $u=0$, and have first derivatives bounded by a fixed multiple of the active dimension, proving the asymptotics. [step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra, construct] ∎

lem-singular-value-product-bound.actual_claim_text:
Let $X\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $Y\in\mathbb F^{n\times q}$, and $Z\in\mathbb F^{r\times m}$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. For every $1\le i\le\min(m,n,q)$ and $1\le j\le\min(r,m,n)$,
$$\sigma_i(XY)\le\sigma_i(X)\|Y\|_2,\qquad \sigma_j(ZX)\le\|Z\|_2\sigma_j(X).$$

current_proof_steps.text: Let $X_{i-1}$ be the rank-at-most-$(i-1)$ SVD truncation in [F1]. Then $X_{i-1}Y$ has rank at most $i-1$, and [F1] applied to $XY$ gives $\sigma_i(XY)\le\|(X-X_{i-1})Y\|_2$. [F1, construct]

For each unit vector $z$, [F2] gives $\|(X-X_{i-1})Yz\|_2\le\|X-X_{i-1}\|_2\|Yz\|_2\le\|X-X_{i-1}\|_2\|Y\|_2$. Taking the supremum over such $z$ and using [F1] yields $\|(X-X_{i-1})Y\|_2\le\sigma_i(X)\|Y\|_2$. Combining with step 1.1 proves the right-multiplication inequality. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

Let $X_{j-1}$ be the rank-at-most-$(j-1)$ SVD truncation of $X$. Then $ZX_{j-1}$ has rank at most $j-1$, so [F1] gives $\sigma_j(ZX)\le\|Z(X-X_{j-1})\|_2$. For every unit vector $v$, [F2] gives $\|Z(X-X_{j-1})v\|_2\le\|Z\|_2\|(X-X_{j-1})v\|_2$. Taking the supremum and using [F1] yields $\|Z(X-X_{j-1})\|_2\le\|Z\|_2\sigma_j(X)$, proving the left-multiplication inequality. [F1, F2, construct] ∎

cases.endpoints: C:The valid indices run from one to the stated minimum dimensions, so the final admissible singular index is included and larger indices are not asserted.

lem-singular-values-lipschitz-in-spectra.actual_claim_text:
Let $A,E\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and put $p=\min(m,n)$. Then for every $1\le i\le p$,
$$|\sigma_i(A+E)-\sigma_i(A)|\le\|E\|_2.$$

current_proof_steps.text: Choose a rank-at-most-$(i-1)$ SVD truncation $A_{i-1}$ of $A$. By [F1] and [F2], $\sigma_i(A+E)\le\|A+E-A_{i-1}\|_2\le\|A-A_{i-1}\|_2+\|E\|_2=\sigma_i(A)+\|E\|_2$. [F1, F2, choose]

Apply step 1.1 with $A+E$ in place of $A$ and $-E$ in place of $E$. This gives $\sigma_i(A)\le\sigma_i(A+E)+\|E\|_2$. The two one-sided inequalities give the stated absolute-value bound. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_notes.subject: Spectral-norm Lipschitz bound for ordered singular values
source_notes.domain: two equal-shape matrices and indices one through the smaller dimension
source_notes.result: each singular-value change is no larger than the perturbation operator norm
source_notes.choice: The matrices and ordered singular values are fixed; a norm inequality, rather than a choice of vector matching, supplies the estimate.

cases.empty: C:At smaller dimension zero the per-index assertion is vacuous; the formula never calls a zeroth or missing singular value.
cases.one: C:For a scalar matrix the claim is the reverse triangle inequality for absolute values, the one-singular-value instance of the same norm bound.
cases.zero: C:For zero perturbation the two singular lists coincide and both sides of the claimed difference bound are zero.
cases.degenerate: C:Rank changes and repeated or zero singular values are admitted; the bound is absolute and does not divide by a singular value.
cases.endpoints: C:The estimate includes the last singular index p; there is no relative-error conclusion requiring it to be positive.

lem-strong-rrqr-column-swap-volume-ratio.actual_claim_text:
Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ have full column rank, $m\ge n$, and let $A\Pi=QR$ be a full QR factorization, with $Q\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ unitary and $R\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ upper trapezoidal. Partition $R=\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ after the first $k$ rows and columns, where $R_{11}\in\mathbb F^{k\times k}$ is nonsingular and $1\le k<n$. Write $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$, $\omega_i=\|e_i^*R_{11}^{-1}\|_2$, and $\gamma_j=\|R_{22}(:,j)\|_2$. Let $J$ be the selected set of $k$ columns and define its volume by $\operatorname{vol}(A(:,J))=\det(A(:,J)^*A(:,J))^{1/2}$. Replacing selected column $i$ by trailing column $j$ changes this volume by the factor
$$\frac{\operatorname{vol}(A(:,(J\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}))}{\operatorname{vol}(A(:,J))}=\bigl(|X_{ij}|^2+(\omega_i\gamma_j)^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$

current_proof_steps.text: Apply $Q^*$ to the selected columns and the candidate trailing column. The selected matrix becomes $C=R_{11}$ in the top $k$ rows. After replacing column $i$, the top block is $C'=R_{11}S$, where $S$ is the identity with column $i$ replaced by column $j$ of $X$; the lower block has only column $i$ nonzero, equal to $c=R_{22}(:,j)$. Hence the replaced Gram matrix is $(C')^*C'+\|c\|_2^2 e_ie_i^*$. If $X_{ij}\ne0$, then $S$ is nonsingular, $\det S=X_{ij}$, and row $i$ of $(C')^{-1}=S^{-1}R_{11}^{-1}$ is row $i$ of $R_{11}^{-1}$ divided by $X_{ij}$. [F1, construct]

For any nonsingular Gram matrix $G$ and vector $u$, factor $G+uu^*=G(I+G^{-1}uu^*)$. Multilinearity of the determinant gives $\det(I+ab^*)=1+b^*a$: terms choosing two updated columns vanish because both are proportional to $a$. Hence $\det(G+uu^*)=\det(G)(1+u^*G^{-1}u)$. Apply this identity to the Gram matrix in step 1.1 with $G=(C')^*C'$ and $u=\|c\|_2e_i$. Since $(C')^{-1}$ has row $i$ equal to row $i$ of $R_{11}^{-1}$ divided by $X_{ij}$, $e_i^*G^{-1}e_i=\omega_i^2/|X_{ij}|^2$. The determinant is therefore $|\det R_{11}|^2|X_{ij}|^2\left(1+\|c\|_2^2\omega_i^2/|X_{ij}|^2\right)=|\det R_{11}|^2\left(|X_{ij}|^2+(\omega_i\gamma_j)^2\right)$. The original selected volume squared is $|\det R_{11}|^2$, so taking the nonnegative square root gives the formula when $X_{ij}\ne0$. [step 1.1, algebra]

Both squared volumes and the right-hand side in step 2.1 are continuous in $X_{ij}$. Perturbing $X_{ij}$ to nonzero values and taking a limit proves the same identity when $X_{ij}=0$. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_notes.subject: The selected-column swap volume identity
source_notes.domain: full-column-rank matrix, nonsingular leading QR block and target from one to n-1
source_notes.result: the volume ratio equals the combined coefficient/residual score
source_notes.choice: Selected and replacement columns are supplied indices; Gram determinants and the finite QR identity specify the ratio uniquely.

cases.empty: N:Target k is at least one and below n, so both selected and trailing index sets are nonempty.
cases.one: C:One selected column is permitted when n exceeds one; its Gram determinant is the squared column norm and the same scalar ratio formula applies.
cases.endpoints: C:Targets one and n-1 are admitted, but k zero and k=n are excluded before forming the inverse leading block and a replacement pair.

prop-spectral-numerical-rank-counts-sing.actual_claim_text:
Let $m,n\ge1$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $p=\min(m,n)$, and $\tau\ge0$. For the spectral norm, the numerical rank defined by [[def-numerical-rank-relative-to-a-norm-scale-and-tolerance]] satisfies
$$\operatorname{rank}_\tau(A)=\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:\sigma_i(A)>\tau\}.$$

current_proof_steps.text: Put $q=\#\{i\le p:\sigma_i(A)>\tau\}$. For every $k<q$, one has $k<p$ and $\sigma_{k+1}(A)\ge\sigma_q(A)>\tau$ (when $q>0$), so [F2] shows that no rank-at-most-$k$ matrix lies within distance $\tau$. If $q<p$, then $\sigma_{q+1}(A)\le\tau$ and the rank-$q$ truncation from [F2] is within distance $\tau$. If $q=p$, [F3] gives $\operatorname{rank}A\le p=q$, so $A$ itself is an admissible matrix at distance zero. Thus the least admissible rank is $q$. [F2, F3, algebra]

By [F1], the least admissible rank is $\operatorname{rank}_\tau(A)$; step 1.1 identifies it with the number of singular values strictly greater than $\tau$. This proves the formula, including $q=0$ and thresholds equal to a singular value. [step 1.1, F1] ∎

source_notes.subject: Spectral numerical rank as the strict singular-value count
source_notes.domain: positive matrix dimensions and nonnegative tolerance
source_notes.result: numerical rank is the count of singular values strictly above tau
source_notes.choice: The finite index set is determined by an ordered singular-value list and a strict comparison; no arbitrary rank-attaining approximation is selected in the count.

cases.empty: N:The Statement requires positive m,n, so the singular-value list contains at least one entry even if none exceeds the tolerance.
cases.one: C:A scalar matrix contributes count one exactly when its modulus exceeds tau; otherwise the strict count is zero.
cases.degenerate: C:Zero and repeated singular values are handled by the strict threshold count, so rank deficiency does not invalidate the identity.

thm-bidiagonal-singular-values-relative-.actual_claim_text:
Let $n\ge1$, and let $B,\widetilde B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ be upper bidiagonal, $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with $0\le\epsilon<1$. Suppose each corresponding nonzero diagonal or superdiagonal entry is multiplied by a scalar whose modulus lies in $[1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]$, and every zero entry remains zero. Put $q=(1+\epsilon)/(1-\epsilon)$. Then $B$ and $\widetilde B$ have the same number of zero singular values, and for each positive singular value in descending order,
$$q^{-2n}\sigma_i(B)\le\sigma_i(\widetilde B)\le q^{2n}\sigma_i(B).$$

This is a relative perturbation theorem. A computed bidiagonal SVD inherits it only when a separate backward-error analysis verifies this componentwise relative assumption; an absolute normwise perturbation estimate by itself is not that verification.

current_proof_steps.text: Write the diagonal ratios as $s_i=\widetilde d_i/d_i$ when $d_i\ne0$, and put $s_i=1$ when $d_i=0$. Write the superdiagonal ratios as $t_i=\widetilde e_i/e_i$ when $e_i\ne0$, and put $t_i=1$ when $e_i=0$. Set $r_1=1$, $\ell_i=s_i/r_i$, and, for $i<n$, set $r_{i+1}=r_i t_i/s_i$. Then $L=\operatorname{diag}(\ell_i)$ and $R=\operatorname{diag}(r_i)$ are invertible and entrywise multiplication gives $\widetilde B=LBR$, including at zero entries because both matrices preserve each zero. [given, construct]

Since $|s_i|,|t_i|\in[1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]$, each ratio $|t_i/s_i|$ lies in $[q^{-1},q]$. Induction gives $q^{-(i-1)}\le|r_i|\le q^{i-1}$. From $\ell_i=s_i/r_i$ and $q(1-\epsilon)=1+\epsilon$, both $|\ell_i|$ and $|\ell_i|^{-1}$ are at most $q^n$; the same bound holds for $|r_i|$ and $|r_i|^{-1}$. By [F2], $\|L\|_2,\|L^{-1}\|_2,\|R\|_2,\|R^{-1}\|_2\le q^n$. [step 1.1, F2, induction, algebra]

First apply the right-multiplication inequality in [F1] to $(LB)R$, then the left-multiplication inequality to $LB$: $\sigma_i(\widetilde B)\le\|R\|_2\sigma_i(LB)\le\|R\|_2\|L\|_2\sigma_i(B)\le q^{2n}\sigma_i(B)$. Applying the same two inequalities to $B=L^{-1}\widetilde B R^{-1}$ gives the reverse bound. Since $L,R$ are invertible, multiplication by them preserves rank; [F3] then shows the zero singular values agree. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F3, algebra]
Step 3.1 proves both inequalities and the zero-value assertion. [step 3.1] ∎

source_notes.subject: Componentwise-relative perturbation of bidiagonal singular values
source_notes.domain: positive bidiagonal order and epsilon in the half-open interval from zero to one
source_notes.result: zero singular-value multiplicity is unchanged and positive values lie between q powers
source_notes.choice: The perturbation multipliers are given entrywise; finite diagonal-scaling arguments bound them without choosing a numerical algorithm output.

cases.empty: N:The order n is explicitly at least one, so this is not an empty bidiagonal matrix theorem.
cases.degenerate: C:Zero entries must remain zero and the number of zero singular values is preserved; the multiplicative estimate is asserted only for the positive singular values.

thm-bidiagonal-svd-backward-error-under-.actual_claim_text:
Let $C_0\in\mathbb F^{M\times p}$, $M\ge p$, be the tall orientation used by [[alg-householder-bidiagonalization]], and let $B_J\in\mathbb F^{p\times p}$ be the final bidiagonal-QR work matrix returned by [[alg-implicit-shifted-bidiagonal-qr-with-deflation]]. Set $C_J=\begin{bmatrix}B_J\\0_{M-p,p}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb F^{M\times p}$. Suppose the computed bidiagonal reduction and QR sweeps perform $J$ stages, each either an elementary left/right unitary update or an identity update for a deflation/cleanup write. At stage $j$, assume the actual active matrix obeys
$$C_j=L_j^*(C_{j-1}+E_j)R_j+D_j,$$
where $L_j,R_j$ are unitary and $\eta_j\ge0$, $\|E_j\|_F\le\eta_j\|C_{j-1}\|_F$, and $D_j$ is the additive representation of entries discarded by deflation or cleanup at that stage, with $\delta_j=\|D_j\|_F$. A deflation/cleanup write is represented by $L_j=R_j=I$, $E_j=0$, and the recorded additive change $D_j$. The deflation record returned by the algorithm identifies each such entry and its old value, so it determines $D_j$. Then the returned tall transformed matrix $C_J$ satisfies
$$C_0+E=L C_J R^*$$
for unitary accumulated factors $L,R$ and some $E$ with
$$\|E\|_F\le\left(\prod_{j=1}^J(1+\eta_j)-1\right)\|C_0\|_F+\sum_{j=1}^J\delta_j\prod_{\ell=j+1}^J(1+\eta_\ell).$$
If no deflation or other cleanup is performed, every $\delta_j=0$. For the successful scaled arithmetic realization [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]], [[lem-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-local-backward-error]] establishes these hypotheses: choose $\eta_j=\eta_H(r_j)$ for Householder updates, $\eta_j=\eta_G$ for Givens updates with an actual target zero write, and its smaller separate-block coefficient when no matrix entry is overwritten. This covers real/complex left and right updates. Every additional discarded entry is included in $D_j$. Rounded dense accumulators remain separate from these exact represented products.

current_proof_steps.text: Iterating the norm inequality from [A1] gives $\|C_j\|_F\le(1+\eta_j)\|C_{j-1}\|_F+\delta_j$. Induction from $C_0$ yields $\|C_j\|_F\le\left(\prod_{r=1}^j(1+\eta_r)\right)\|C_0\|_F+\sum_{r=1}^j\delta_r\prod_{s=r+1}^j(1+\eta_s)$: the base case $j=0$ is equality, and the one-step inequality multiplies every prior term by $1+\eta_j$ and adds $\delta_j$. [A1, F3, induction, algebra]

Unwind each update in the accumulated unitary coordinates supplied by [F1]–[F2]. The original-input perturbation is the sum of each $E_j$ and each $D_j$ transported by products of later unitary factors. Unitary left/right multiplication preserves Frobenius norm, so $\|E\|_F\le\sum_{j=1}^J\eta_j\|C_{j-1}\|_F+\sum_{j=1}^J\delta_j$. Substitute step 1.1. For the $C_0$ terms, $\sum_j\eta_j\prod_{r<j}(1+\eta_r)=\prod_r(1+\eta_r)-1$. For a fixed $\delta_i$, its contribution is $\delta_i\left(1+\sum_{j>i}\eta_j\prod_{i<r<j}(1+\eta_r)\right)=\delta_i\prod_{r>i}(1+\eta_r)$. These identities give the stated bound. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

The same coordinate unwinding gives $C_J= L^*(C_0+E)R$ for products $L,R$ of the unitary update factors, hence $C_0+E=L C_JR^*$. Step 2.1 gives its error bound; setting every $\delta_j=0$ gives the no-deflation case. [step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra]

For the specified finite-precision algorithm, apply [F5] to each actual update, retaining its range and active-dimension hypotheses. It gives exactly [A1], including each target-zero write. Deflation and any additional discarded entries remain $D_j$, so steps 1.1, 2.1, and 3.1 prove the displayed aggregate bound for the concrete implementation. Shift rounding affects which rotation is chosen, not the validity of its unitary backward-error certificate; no unconditional convergence is asserted. [F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_notes.subject: Accumulation of local bidiagonal-SVD backward errors
source_notes.domain: actual elementary unitary updates and every recorded additive deflation/cleanup change
source_notes.result: a global represented-unitary reconstruction with product local-error and propagated additive-discard terms
source_notes.choice: The actual local transformation lists and discarded entries are given; the proof propagates that concrete finite stage sequence.

cases.endpoints: C:At a final deflation stage the remaining product over later updates is the empty product one; every discarded old entry is still retained in the additive term.

thm-strong-rrqr-singular-value-compariso.actual_claim_text:
Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ have full column rank, $m\ge n$, and let the exact-arithmetic version of [[alg-strong-rank-revealing-qr-with-finite-swaps]] return `success` with full QR factorization
$$A\Pi=Q\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix},$$
where $Q\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ is unitary and the displayed $R$ is upper trapezoidal with $m$ rows. Let the target satisfy $0\le k<n$ and the factor satisfy $f\ge1$. For $1\le k<n$, assume $R_{11}\in\mathbb F^{k\times k}$ is nonsingular and put $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$. Put $g=(1+f^2k(n-k))^{1/2}$. Then
$$\sigma_i(R_{11})\ge\frac{\sigma_i(A)}{g}\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad \sigma_j(R_{22})\le g\,\sigma_{k+j}(A)\quad(1\le j\le n-k).$$
For $k=0$, the second comparison is the equality $R_{22}=Q^*A\Pi$ with $g=1$. These conclusions use the combined score in the algorithm; the bound on $X$ alone is not used as a substitute for control of $R_{22}$. For a computed candidate $\widehat R$ with the algorithm's verified certificate $(W,(b_{ij}),\varepsilon)$, put $\widetilde A=W\widehat R\Pi^*$. No full-column-rank assumption on $\widetilde A$ is required beyond nonsingularity of $\widehat R_{11}$ when $k>0$. Then the corresponding residual-adjusted bounds are
$$\sigma_i(\widehat R_{11})\ge\frac{\sigma_i(A)-\varepsilon}{g}\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad \sigma_j(\widehat R_{22})\le g\bigl(\sigma_{k+j}(A)+\varepsilon\bigr)\quad(1\le j\le n-k).$$
For $k=0$, these reduce to $\sigma_j(\widehat R)\le\sigma_j(A)+\varepsilon$. Computed scores alone do not certify either conclusion.

current_proof_steps.text:
If $k=0$, then $R_{22}=Q^*A\Pi$ and both $Q$ and $\Pi$ are unitary, so they preserve singular values; the stated case follows. Assume henceforth $1\le k<n$. Write $A_0=R_{11}$, $C=R_{22}$, and $X=A_0^{-1}R_{12}$. Summing the $k(n-k)$ inequalities in [F1] gives
$$\|X\|_F^2+\|A_0^{-1}\|_F^2\|C\|_F^2\le f^2k(n-k).$$
Indeed, $\sum_i\omega_i^2=\|A_0^{-1}\|_F^2$ and $\sum_j\gamma_j^2=\|C\|_F^2$. [F1, F3, algebra]

Since $A$ has full column rank and $k<n$, $C$ has full column rank: if $Cz=0$ for nonzero $z$, then $R\binom{-A_0^{-1}R_{12}z}{z}=0$, contradicting full column rank of $R=Q^*A\Pi$, which has the same rank as $A$ by [F3]. Thus $\alpha=\|C\|_2/\sigma_k(A_0)>0$. Since $\sigma_k(A_0)=1/\|A_0^{-1}\|_2$, one has $\alpha^2=\|C\|_2^2\|A_0^{-1}\|_2^2\le\|C\|_F^2\|A_0^{-1}\|_F^2$, so step 1.1 gives $\|X\|_F^2+\alpha^2\le f^2k(n-k)$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra]

By [F3], $R=Q^*A\Pi$ has the same singular values as $A$. Define $D_1=\operatorname{diag}(A_0,C/\alpha)$ and $W_1=\begin{bmatrix}I_k&X\\0&\alpha I_{n-k}\end{bmatrix}$, so $R=D_1W_1$. For vectors $x,y$, $\|W_1(x,y)\|_2^2=\|x+Xy\|_2^2+\alpha^2\|y\|_2^2$ is bounded by the quadratic form of $M_1=\begin{bmatrix}1&\|X\|_2\\\|X\|_2&\|X\|_2^2+\alpha^2\end{bmatrix}$ at $(\|x\|_2,\|y\|_2)$. For scalars $u,v$ its quadratic form is $(u+\|X\|_2v)^2+\alpha^2v^2\ge0$, so it is positive semidefinite and its largest eigenvalue is at most its trace; thus $\|W_1\|_2^2\le1+\|X\|_F^2+\alpha^2\le g^2$. Since $\|C/\alpha\|_2=\sigma_k(A_0)$, the ordered first $k$ singular values of $D_1$ are those of $A_0$. By [F2], $\sigma_i(R)\le\sigma_i(D_1)\|W_1\|_2$, proving $\sigma_i(A_0)\ge\sigma_i(A)/g$ for $i\le k$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]

Define $D_2=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha A_0,C)$ and $W_2=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha I_k&-X\\0&I_{n-k}\end{bmatrix}$, so $D_2=RW_2$. For vectors $x,y$, $\|W_2(x,y)\|_2^2=\|\alpha x-Xy\|_2^2+\|y\|_2^2$ is bounded by the quadratic form of $M_2=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha^2&\alpha\|X\|_2\\\alpha\|X\|_2&\|X\|_2^2+1\end{bmatrix}$ at $(\|x\|_2,\|y\|_2)$. Its determinant is $\alpha^2>0$ and its diagonal entries are positive, so it is positive semidefinite; its largest eigenvalue is at most its trace. Thus $\|W_2\|_2^2\le1+\|X\|_F^2+\alpha^2\le g^2$. The smallest singular value of $\alpha A_0$ is $\|C\|_2$, so the first $k$ singular values of $D_2$ are those of $\alpha A_0$ and its remaining $n-k$ singular values are those of $C$. Therefore $\sigma_j(C)=\sigma_{k+j}(D_2)\le\sigma_{k+j}(R)\|W_2\|_2\le g\sigma_{k+j}(A)$ by [F2] and [F3]. [step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]

The preceding block proof also applies to any upper trapezoidal $R$ whose $R_{11}$ is nonsingular and whose exact combined scores are at most $f$, even when $R$ is rank deficient. If $C\ne0$, $\alpha>0$ and steps 2.1–3.2 apply without the full-column-rank argument. If $C=0$, write $R=\operatorname{diag}(A_0,0)\begin{bmatrix}I&X\\0&I\end{bmatrix}$. Directly $R=A_0[I\;X]$ with zero lower rows and $\|[I\;X]\|_2^2=1+\|X\|_2^2\le g^2$. The product bound proves the first comparison, and the second is $0\le g\sigma_{k+j}(R)$. Thus the certificate gives both comparisons with $A$ replaced by $\widetilde A$ and blocks $\widehat R_{11},\widehat R_{22}$. Since $\|A-\widetilde A\|_2\le\varepsilon$, [F4] gives $\sigma_i(\widetilde A)\ge\sigma_i(A)-\varepsilon$ and $\sigma_{k+j}(\widetilde A)\le\sigma_{k+j}(A)+\varepsilon$. Combining proves the computed bounds. The $k=0$ case follows directly from unitary invariance and [F4]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, F2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

source_notes.subject: Exact and certified-computed strong RRQR spectral comparisons
source_notes.domain: full QR exact success or a represented-unitary computed score/residual certificate
source_notes.result: leading/trailing singular-value bounds, with reconstruction epsilon retained for computed data
source_notes.choice: The certificate fixes W and the returned blocks, while each exact score bound is rigorously supplied rather than inferred from rounded tests.

cases.empty: C:For target k zero there are no leading-block scores or inverse conditions; the trailing comparison reduces to the unitary full factor and the stated epsilon allowance.
cases.one: C:One selected column is valid when n is greater than one; with n one only the explicitly handled k-zero branch is admissible.
cases.endpoints: C:The bounds include f equal to one and targets from zero through n-1; neither a target n nor an uncertified rounded score triggers the spectral conclusion.

thm-strong-rrqr-swap-rule-terminates.actual_claim_text: For a full-column-rank $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $m\ge n$, $0\le k<n$, and $f\ge1$, run the exact-arithmetic version of [[alg-strong-rank-revealing-qr-with-finite-swaps]]. For $k=0$ the algorithm returns `success` without swaps. For $1\le k<n$, every accepted swap strictly increases the volume of the selected $k$ columns. Therefore the procedure makes at most $\binom nk-1$ swaps and returns `success` if its cap is at least that number. On exact-arithmetic success with $k\ge1$, every score is at most $f$ and hence $\max_{i,j}|(R_{11}^{-1}R_{12})_{ij}|\le f$. If a smaller cap is reached while a violation remains, it returns `swap-budget-exhausted`; a smaller cap can still suffice when the criterion is met earlier.

current_proof_steps.text: If $k=0$, the algorithm's first branch returns `success` without a swap. Assume $1\le k<n$. Every accepted swap has score strictly greater than $f\ge1$. By [F2] it multiplies the selected volume by a factor strictly greater than one. Thus the selected volume strictly increases at each swap, so no selected subset can recur because its volume is determined by the fixed input matrix and subset. [F1, F2, algebra]

For $1\le k<n$, there are exactly $\binom nk$ possible selected $k$-column subsets. The initial subset has positive volume by full column rank, and by step 1.1 no subset can recur after a strict increase. If $\binom nk-1$ swaps have occurred, all $\binom nk$ subsets have therefore been visited; a remaining violation would prescribe another swap to an already visited subset, contradicting step 1.1. Thus a cap at least $\binom nk-1$ cannot be reached with a violation remaining, and the algorithm returns success. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

For $k=0$ the coefficient assertion is vacuous. For $1\le k<n$, success gives $s_{ij}\le f$ for all pairs. Since $|X_{ij}|\le s_{ij}$ by the score definition, $\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|\le f$. If a smaller cap is reached while a violation remains, the algorithm returns `swap-budget-exhausted`; if no violation remains first, it returns success. [F1, algebra] ∎

source_notes.subject: Finite strong-RRQR swaps from strictly increasing selected volume
source_notes.domain: full-column-rank input, target below n and f at least one
source_notes.result: at most binomial(n,k)-one accepted swaps, with explicit insufficient-cap status
source_notes.choice: There are finitely many selected subsets and each accepted pair has the algorithm lexicographic rule; no infinite sequence of arbitrary swaps is chosen.

cases.empty: C:The k-zero branch returns success with no swap, so no volume ratio or selected-column inverse is required.
cases.one: C:At k one the finitely many selected subsets are the n columns; if n is one only k zero is allowed and no swap is needed.
cases.endpoints: C:A score strictly above f causes a swap, so equality at f is acceptable even when f is one; a smaller cap can still succeed before any violation remains.

thm-svd-thresholded-least-squares-minimu.actual_claim_text:
Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and $\tau\ge0$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. Let $A=U\Sigma V^*$ be an exact SVD. Define $\Sigma_\tau$ by retaining $\sigma_i$ when $\sigma_i>\tau$ and replacing each $\sigma_i\le\tau$ by zero, and set $A_\tau=U\Sigma_\tau V^*$. Put $q=\#\{i:\sigma_i>\tau\}$, the spectral numerical rank of $A$ at threshold $\tau$. The output $x_\tau=A_\tau^+b$ of [[alg-rank-thresholded-least-squares-by-svd]] is the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm least-squares solution for the truncated model $A_\tau x\approx b$. Moreover,
$$\|A-A_\tau\|_2=\sigma_{q+1}\le\tau,\qquad \|Ax_\tau-b\|_2\le\|A_\tau x_\tau-b\|_2+\tau\|x_\tau\|_2,$$
with $\sigma_{p+1}=0$ when $q=p=\min(m,n)$. If every discarded singular value is zero, then $A_\tau=A$ and $x_\tau$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares solution for the original matrix. If a positive singular value is discarded, no original-matrix least-squares optimality is asserted.

current_proof_steps.text: Let $I=\{i\le p:\sigma_i>\tau\}$. By [F1]–[F2], $A_\tau=\sum_{i\in I}\sigma_i u_i v_i^*$ and $A_\tau^+=\sum_{i\in I}\sigma_i^{-1}v_i u_i^*$. Orthonormality gives $A_\tau A_\tau^+=\sum_{i\in I}u_i u_i^*$ and $A_\tau^+A_\tau=\sum_{i\in I}v_i v_i^*$, which are self-adjoint. Using $u_i^*u_j=v_i^*v_j=\delta_{ij}$ in those sums verifies the two Penrose product equations. Together with self-adjointness, these are the four equations; by [F6], $A_\tau^+$ is the unique Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse of $A_\tau$. The calculation includes $I=\varnothing$, when both matrices and sums are zero. [F1, F2, F6, algebra]
By [F5], $q$ is the spectral numerical rank retained by the strict threshold. The SVD truncation and [F4] give $\|A-A_\tau\|_2=\sigma_{q+1}\le\tau$; when $q=p$, the tail is zero. [F4, F5, F7]
Apply [F3] to $M=A_\tau$. Its unique minimum-norm least-squares solution is $A_\tau^+b=x_\tau$, proving the truncated-model claim. [step 1.1, F3]

By [F7], $\|(A-A_\tau)x_\tau\|_2\le\|A-A_\tau\|_2\|x_\tau\|_2$; [F8] gives $\|Ax_\tau-b\|_2\le\|A_\tau x_\tau-b\|_2+\|(A-A_\tau)x_\tau\|_2$. Combining with step 1.2 proves the stated residual bound. [step 1.2, F7, F8, algebra]

If every discarded singular value is zero, the SVD formula gives $A=A_\tau$, so step 2.1 is the original-matrix solution. If any positive singular value is discarded, the proof has established optimality only for $A_\tau$; it supplies no normal-equation or minimum-residual claim for $A$. [step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]
Steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2, and 3.1 prove all stated claims and the limitation. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

source_notes.subject: Minimum-norm least squares for the declared truncated SVD model
source_notes.domain: an exact SVD and nonnegative strict-retention threshold
source_notes.result: a unique minimum-norm model solution with tail and original-residual comparison
source_notes.choice: The truncated pseudoinverse is canonical once the exact SVD model is supplied; no arbitrary null-space component is appended.
